question: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.

In my first internship, I pushed a small config change that broke the dev build for two hours. I realized it after the fact and could have just reverted quietly, but I posted in the team channel what I changed, why it failed, and the rollback.
My mentor thanked me and said it saved them time debugging. I also updated the runbook so the same mistake wouldn't happen again.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.
Intern: pushed config change that broke dev build for 2 hrs
Posted in channel with exact change and rollback instead of silent revert
Quote: "I realized I could just fix it quietly but didn't want someone else wasting time"
Follow-up: reaction - mentor thanked her and she updated the runbook
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate described a small-scope error in their own change and chose to surface it in the team channel rather than revert silently. The concrete action was posting the exact change and rollback. This shows early ownership and coachability on individual work. The follow-up confirmed the team viewed the transparency positively and she added a runbook entry. Biggest strength is choosing visibility over convenience on a low-stakes mistake.

lowerTranscript.text: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.
I once had a test that was flaky and I just commented it out. Later the team found out and I said it was temporary.
Did you tell anyone before they noticed?
No, I figured it would get fixed in the next sprint so I didn't raise it.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.
Commented out flaky test without telling anyone
Only acknowledged after team discovered it
Quote: "I figured it would get fixed in the next sprint"
Follow-up: no proactive disclosure
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The candidate described hiding a change that affected the test suite and only acknowledged it after discovery. No evidence of voluntary disclosure or learning from the choice. The follow-up confirmed the absence of any attempt to surface the issue early. This signals limited ownership on even small individual work. Biggest gap is treating transparency as optional rather than default.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.
I approved a shared library change that introduced a regression for two downstream teams. Once I saw the impact I scheduled a cross-team sync, owned the decision, and walked through the fix timeline.
Why not just fix it quietly?
The other teams were already debugging and I didn't want them chasing the wrong cause. I also updated the review checklist so similar changes would be caught earlier.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.
Approved library change causing regression for two downstream teams
Called cross-team sync and owned the root cause instead of silent fix
Quote: "They were already debugging so I didn't want them chasing the wrong cause"
Follow-up: updated review checklist to prevent recurrence
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate owned a change that affected multiple teams and proactively scheduled a cross-team sync rather than attempting a quiet fix. The action included walking through the timeline and updating a shared checklist. This demonstrates influence without authority on a cross-team issue. The follow-up showed a concrete process improvement. Biggest strength is choosing transparency that reduced wasted effort for others.

lowerTranscript.text: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.
There was a metrics dashboard change that produced wrong numbers for a week. I fixed the query and mentioned it in the next team meeting.
Did the consuming teams know the numbers were off?
I assumed they would notice eventually so I didn't send a direct note.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.

Fixed quietly and mentioned only in next internal meeting
Quote: "I assumed they would notice eventually"
Follow-up: no direct notification to consuming teams
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate described a cross-team impact but chose minimal disclosure after the fact. No evidence of proactive outreach to affected teams. The follow-up confirmed the assumption that others would self-detect the issue. This shows limited cross-team influence and incomplete ownership. Biggest gap is treating transparency as an internal team matter only.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.
My team missed a committed date because I had understaffed the project. I told the leadership team the miss was my call on resourcing and laid out the recovery plan with new headcount asks.
I also told the team directly that the pressure came from my estimation error and adjusted their scope for the next quarter.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.
Missed committed date due to understaffing decision
Told leadership the miss was their resourcing call, not team's execution
Quote: "The pressure came from my estimation error"
Follow-up: adjusted team scope and communicated directly to them
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate took public responsibility for a resourcing decision that caused a date miss and communicated it both upward and to the team. The actions included owning the miss in leadership review and adjusting team scope afterward. This shows ownership of team outcomes and protection of the team. The follow-up confirmed direct feedback to the team. Biggest strength is modeling accountability at the team level.

manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The candidate shifted focus to team execution rather than owning their own resourcing or priority decisions. This signals weak team ownership and limited integrity under pressure. Biggest gap is protecting self at the expense of the team.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.

I green-lit a market expansion that consumed significant capital before we saw traction was not materializing. In the next board meeting I walked through the original thesis, the data that disproved it, and the decision to wind down the effort.
They asked for the learning and later referenced the transparency when we made another large bet. We also published a short internal note so other teams could avoid the same pattern.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of admitting a mistake openly even though you could have hidden it or minimized it.
Green-lit market expansion that burned capital with no traction
Told board the original thesis was wrong and the wind-down decision
Quote: "I walked through the data that disproved the thesis"
Follow-up: board referenced the transparency on later bets; internal note published
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate publicly reversed a high-stakes strategic decision in front of the board and shared the disconfirming data. The action included stating the original thesis was incorrect and publishing an internal note. This demonstrates strategic judgment and long-term org learning. The follow-up showed downstream effects on board trust and other teams. Biggest strength is treating a visible failure as an opportunity for organizational transparency.
